newsitem.title: UK: ICCO puts world 96/97 cocoa deficit at 134,000 T.
newsitem.headline: ICCO puts world 96/97 cocoa deficit at 134,000 T.

text.p: The International Cocoa Organisation (ICCO) said on Thursday the world's 1996/97 cocoa production deficit should be 134,000 tonnes compared with its earlier estimate of 115,000 tonnes .
That compares with 1995/96's surplus of a revised 155,000 tonnes (previously 160,000 tonnes).
It also cut its 1996/97 cocoa bean production estimate by 20,000 tonnes from its previous forecast made in March to 2.695 million tonnes.

The London-based ICCO said the overall decline reflected, on one hand, downward revision made for Malaysia (down 15,000 to 100,000 tonnes), Ghana (down 5,000 to 330,000), the Dominican Republic (down 5,000 to 55,000) and Papua New Guinea (down 3,000 to 35,000).
On the other hand, the upward revisions were for Nigeria (up 5,000 to 155,000) and Peru (up 4,000 to 15,000 tonnes).
But it kept the forecast for Ivory Coast at 1.125 million tonnes for 1996/97. This compares with an estimated 1.20 million for 1995/96.
The Brazilian crop could reach 165,000 tonnes, up from 230.7 million.
World grindings of cocoa beans in 1996/97 were now forecast at 2.802 million tonnes, a 1,000-tonne reduction from the figure published in March, but nevertheless, a new all-time record level.

On an individual country basis, grinding forecasts had been revised downward for Germany (down 15,000 to 240,000 tonnes), Malaysia (down 5,000 to 95,000) and Belgium/Luxembourg (down 4,000 to 76,000).

On the other hand, grinding forecasts had been increased for the Netherlands (up 5,000 to 400,000 tonnes), the United States (up 5,000 to 370,000), Ivory Coast (up 5,000 to 165,000) and Ecuador (up 5,000 to 45,000).
The ICCO said on the basis of these forecasts, the 1996/97 cocoa year is projected to yield a production deficit amounting to 134,000 tonens, 19,000 tonnes higher than the figure published in March.

The total statistical stocks of cocoa beans at the end of the 1996/97 cocoa year should therefore decline to 1.253 million, which is equivalent to 44.7 percent or just below 5-1/2 months of projected annual world grindings in the year.

Excluding the ICCO buffer stock holding of 26,000 tonnes at the end of the 1996/97 cocoa year, the total stocks directly overhanging the world market would amount to 1.227 million tonnes or just above five months of estimated world grindings in the year.
